candidate.answerReason: A number is divisible by 3 precisely when its digit sum is divisible by 3. Omitting 1 or 4 gives digit sums 9 or 6, and each of the four omitted digits is equally likely.

methods.label: Track the digit left in the bag
methods.explanation:
Divisibility by \(3\) depends only on the sum of the digits, so their order does not affect whether the number wins. The four available digits sum to
\[
1+2+3+4=10.
\]
Omitting \(1,2,3,4\) gives digit sums \(9,8,7,6\), respectively. Only \(9\) and \(6\) are multiples of \(3\), so the favorable omitted digits are \(1\) and \(4\).

Each omitted digit leaves three distinct digits, which can be drawn in \(3\times2\times1=6\) orders. All these ordered draws are equally likely. Every draw omits exactly one digit, so the four groups are disjoint, exhaustive, and equal in size. There are no leading-zero exceptions because all available digits are nonzero.

Two of the four equally likely groups are favorable, giving probability
\[
\frac24=\boxed{\frac12},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
methods.levelReason: The solution uses the elementary digit-sum test and a small sequential count, with no permutation formulas.

candidate.annotationRationale: The targets are divisibility by three and favorable-over-total probability. Without-replacement sampling and equal likelihood support the model. The multiplication principle is method-specific: it proves that each omitted-digit group has the same six ordered outcomes.

review.mathematicalCheck: Omitting digits 1, 2, 3, and 4 produces digit sums 9, 8, 7, and 6. Exactly two groups are favorable. Each omitted digit corresponds to six equally likely ordered draws, so the probability is 12/24=1/2.
